title: How to Run a LinkedIn Outreach Campaign for Freshly Funded Engineering Teams in 2026

## Step 2: Refine and qualify the list


A freshly funded engineering team is not automatically a good prospect. You need to cut the noise before putting anyone into a LinkedIn sequence.


I segment the list into three buckets before drafting messages.


**Tier 1 — High intent.** VP Engineering, CTO, or Head of Platform at a Series A or B company that raised $10M–$50M within the last 60 days, with 20–100 employees and active job posts for platform/infrastructure engineers.


**Tier 2 — Active build-out.** Head of Infrastructure, Director of Engineering, or Staff/Principal engineer at a company that raised $5M–$20M in the last 90 days. Smaller team, but the leader likely owns the build-vs-buy decision.


**Tier 3 — Influence, not final sign-off.** Engineering managers or tech leads at funded teams. They won’t sign a contract, but they can champion internally.


What “qualified” looks like for this audience:


- Funding round closed within the last 90 days. Beyond that, the budget urgency fades.
- Engineering team between 8 and 60 people. Smaller teams are still in survival mode. Much larger teams usually have procurement and longer sales cycles.
- The contact is a technical decision maker or strong influence, not a generic founder unless the company has no VP Eng.
- The company is hiring for platform, DevOps, infrastructure, SRE, or backend roles. That is the clearest buying trigger.
- The company’s tech stack or job posts mention scaling pain: CI/CD, observability, cloud costs, reliability, developer velocity, or security.


Remove anyone who does not have an active engineering role or recent LinkedIn activity. No point running a sequence to a dead profile.


In[Origami](https://origami.chat/) , you can review each contact’s enriched profile while you work. Title, company, headcount, funding stage, location, and tools used are all on the same screen. You don’t have to flip tabs or cross-reference LinkedIn.


A final filter that saves time: keep only contacts who are active on LinkedIn within the last 30 days. If someone hasn’t posted, commented, or changed roles recently, they’re less likely to respond.


For this campaign, a clean list of 100–200 Tier 1 and Tier 2 contacts beats 2,000 mixed titles every time.


## Step 3: Create the LinkedIn sequence


[Origami](https://origami.chat/) gives you two ways to build the sequence.


**Option 1: Paste your own templates.** Write your own 3-touch sequence and paste the templates directly into[Origami](https://origami.chat/) ’s LinkedIn sequencer. Set the delays between touches — Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, or any cadence you want — and hit launch.


**Option 2: Let the agent write it.** Ask the[Origami](https://origami.chat/) AI agent to generate a personalized 3-day LinkedIn sequence for all your leads automatically. The agent writes each message based on the lead’s profile data — title, company, industry — so every message feels custom.


If you’re running this for the first time, use the sequence below. It’s written for freshly funded engineering teams, and you can paste it directly into the sequencer.


### Day 1 — Connection request + note


**Subject line:** Post-raise infra hiring


**Note:**


> Congrats on the recent raise, . I work with post-funding engineering teams that need to scale infrastructure without slowing down feature delivery or burning out the team. Quick question: are you currently hiring platform or infrastructure engineers, or planning a reliability push this quarter? I’d love to follow your team’s build-out.


*Customization note:* If the lead is a VP Eng, keep the message as-is. If they’re a CTO, swap the last line to “I’d love to compare notes on what you’re prioritizing this quarter.” If they’re a Head of Platform, make the pain more specific: “what’s on the platform roadmap now that the raise is closed?”


### Day 3 — Follow-up message


**Subject line:** Developer velocity after a raise


> Hi , saw your team is hiring for a senior platform engineer — that usually means the “just get it done” phase is ending and reliability work is starting to compete with shipping. If you’re like most teams three months post-raise, you’re probably deciding what to build versus buy for CI/CD, observability, or cloud cost control. Would it be useful to see how similar teams handled that after their Series A/B? I can send over a short writeup.


This message works because it references their actual hiring signal and names the exact tension. It doesn’t ask for a meeting. It offers proof.


### Day 7 — Final message


**Subject line:** Closing the loop


> Hi , last one from me. Most freshly funded engineering teams I talk to are under pressure to show board-level progress in 90 days: faster onboarding, fewer incidents, or clearer infrastructure costs. If that’s on your plate, I’m happy to share a 15-minute teardown of what we’re seeing work at companies that just raised. No pitch if it’s not a fit. Want me to send over a few examples?


This is a soft close. It’s not “are you ready to buy?” It’s “want to see how similar teams are solving this?” That’s the right ask for this audience.


### Why this sequence works for freshly funded engineering teams


- It acknowledges the funding event without being sycophantic.
- It ties to a hiring signal, not a generic “I saw you viewed my profile.”
- It names the actual post-raise tension: speed versus stability.
- It offers something small and useful, not a demo.
- It respects the reader’s inbox with a clear end date.


If you want a second sequence for Tier 3 leads, use a shorter Day 1 note and make Day 3 the only follow-up. But for Tier 1 and Tier 2, the three-touch version above is the one I’d run.

### What response rate to expect


Freshly funded engineering teams are a warm-but-saturated audience. They get hit by a lot of sellers after a funding announcement. A clean, well-segmented list with verified contacts and a tight sequence should realistically produce:


- 15–25% connection acceptance rate
- 8–15% reply rate on accepted connections
- 2–5% booked meetings from the original list


If you’re below 15% connection acceptance after 100 invites, your first touch is off or your list has wrong titles. If acceptance is good but replies are low, your Day 3 message isn’t landing. If replies are positive but meetings aren’t booked, your Day 7 CTA is too vague or too heavy.


### When to iterate messaging vs. iterate the list


One mistake I see constantly is treating underperformance as a list problem when it’s actually a message problem.


**Iterate on messaging first if:**


- Connection acceptance is above 20%, but replies are under 5%.
- Replies are price objections or “not right now” from good-fit titles.
- Open rates are normal but click rates are low.


**Iterate on the list if:**


- Connection acceptance is below 15%.
- You get “wrong person” or “I’m not involved in infra” replies.
- Titles match, but company size or funding stage is off.
- A specific segment, like Seed vs Series A, performs much worse.


Start with 50–100 Tier 1 contacts. Run the sequence. Read every negative reply. Adjust either the list filters in[Origami](https://origami.chat/) or the Day 3 message. Don’t blast 1,000 contacts on day one.
